1:
The opening line is a title, and the voices treat it as one. Wesley makes it the heading of all that follows to the end but one, against foreign nations throughout. Gill prefers concerning the nations to against them, and notes that the oracles are uniformly against, never in favour. Ellicott sees traces of a plan: pieces concerned only with outside nations were collected as an appendix, most developing what an earlier chapter gave in outline. Calvin makes the same point, that the volume was formed without the sequence of time being kept, these threats having been uttered long before.

Keil and Delitzsch set the collection beside its predecessors. In one earlier prophet the oracles on six neighbouring peoples merely clear the ground for judgment on Judah, teaching that the world opposed to God must be judged before his kingdom advances; in another the thought is that every apostate kingdom shall be humbled and driven to take refuge with the God of Israel. Henry states it more simply, that God is King and Judge of nations and will call to account those who take no notice of him, and adds the antithesis: here the word of the Lord against the Gentiles, in the later covenant the word for them.

Egypt comes first for reasons the voices share. Gill says it was first accomplished and that the Jews had leaned on Egypt heavily; Henry that the Egyptians were Israel's old oppressors and late deceivers. Clarke divides the chapter into two prophecies, one before the engagement in which the Egyptians were routed, the other belonging to an invasion long after the fall of Jerusalem, and remarks that these chapters far excel their predecessors in majesty and elegance.

The history behind the oracle is filled in. Clarke traces the campaign: the Egyptian king defeated the army of the good king who died of his wound, beat the Babylonians, took the fortress on the great river and garrisoned it, before the Babylonian prince retook it with immense slaughter. Calvin supplies the alliances: the Egyptian marched to help the Assyrians, and the king of Judah, whose house had long been friendly with Babylon, went out against him and fell. Ellicott identifies the Egyptian as the last of the great native sovereigns, sixth of his dynasty, and leaves the site of the fortress disputed.

The muster is a herald's cry, and most of the voices hear irony in it. Calvin explains the device: prophets do not narrate but stage the scene and lend their voice to other persons, here to the Egyptian king's crier. Gill thinks the command addressed to the Egyptian army rather than the Chaldean, and heard from God, who bids them do their utmost and come to nothing; Clarke calls it the summons to a general armament. The equipment is glossed closely: Gill and Calvin distinguish the greater shield from the horseman's lighter buckler, Calvin noting that chariots were then the manner of fighting, while Clarke derives the verb for polishing from the French and calls the mail overlapping scales, which Wesley calls simply coats of mail.

Then the whole display collapses in a line. Keil and Delitzsch mark the suddenness: the host advances well arrayed and the seer at once perceives it terror-stricken and in flight, the question registering an incomprehensible turn; they read the words as an independent exclamation and take the cry of terror round about as perhaps the answer from God's side. Ellicott finds in that cry one of the prophet's characteristic formulae, and pictures the army driven back on the river. Clarke presses the incongruity of so well-appointed a force panic-struck, its commanders beaten down while rallying it. Calvin gives the reason: judged by outward splendour they must have been reckoned victors, but the prophet is set on a watch-tower, from which what looked formidable is frail.
6:
The line about the swift is ambiguous and the voices split over it. Gill gives both readings, a prohibition and a flat future, and prefers the second: neither nimble heels nor stout hearts get anyone out. Calvin allows that the particle is often prohibitive but judges the future more consistent, God declaring that speed and courage avail nothing; Clarke says simply that not even the swiftest shall escape. Calvin notes that the prophets habitually call the Chaldeans northerners, a usage holding even here, where Egyptians are addressed; Wesley fixes the stumbling at the fortress by the river.

Then the army is a river in flood. Gill draws the figure from the annual overflow and finds in it numbers, noise, and force threatening to carry all before it; Clarke compares a river swollen in harvest, a fine image for the incursion of vast armies. Keil and Delitzsch treat the astonished question as one that gets its own answer, the hosts covering the land like that river's waves. Calvin explains why the question is asked: it is put according to the common judgment of men, and meets the doubt of the godly, who reckon strongholds a security and leave God's power out of account. This king triumphed before he fought.

The muster of allies is the same irony. Gill takes the call to horses and chariots as God's, ironically bidding cavalry and charioteers come on; Keil and Delitzsch read it as before, let the host approach and perish nonetheless, and argue from the parallelism that the horses are told to prance, not to be mounted. The auxiliaries are identified variously. Clarke takes the first name for the Arabs bordering Egypt near the eastern sea and the second for Libyans, and reports a contention that the third were bowmen. Ellicott makes the first the peoples of the upper valley, at times independent and now subject, and the second an African people named everywhere as ally or tributary of Egypt. Calvin's point is that hired troops from every quarter made the prophecy incredible.

The reversal is stated as a day and a sacrifice. Gill says it would be not their day but the Lord's, who commands every army. Clarke sees a mighty sacrifice with innumerable victims; Ellicott, borrowing from earlier prophets, makes Egypt the victim and the river bank the altar. Keil and Delitzsch supply the ground: the Egyptians had sinned against the people of God not merely of late, killing their king, carrying off one successor and making a vassal of the next, but from the earliest times. Calvin fastens on the same recent crime, and adds that naming the Egyptians God's adversaries consoled the chosen people; Wesley reduces the drunken sword to a figure for slaughter.

The balm is the sharpest stroke. Gill notes the region's fame for its healing gum; Clarke calls the counsel an irony and the wound incurable, the figure the more pointed because the Egyptians were long celebrated for medicine. Ellicott hears triumphant irony, notes that the balm passed for a cure of all wounds, and finds a second sarcasm in the title virgin, the nation having boasted itself unconquered. Keil and Delitzsch press that title the same way, a people not hitherto forced and now violated. Calvin is careful about the extent: the nation did not perish, but the kingdom was so depressed that it kept within its borders and brought out its forces no more, falling under Babylon soon after.

The last verse reports it done, the battle and its fame related as accomplished. Calvin explains why the report would travel: a small loss goes unnoticed, but when one engagement changes a nation the event is proclaimed everywhere; the cry he takes for lamentation. On the stumbling, Keil and Delitzsch render hero against hero, one over another in confused flight; Wesley agrees that those in front and those behind went down together.
13:
A second oracle begins, and the voices agree it is separate. Gill distinguishes them by scope: the first concerned an army overthrown at one place, this the destruction of the land some years later, dated by a rabbinic chronicle to the twenty-seventh year of the Babylonian's reign. Ellicott agrees and thinks it delivered much later, placed here with the Egyptian series. Keil and Delitzsch notice an unusual formula in the heading and suggest the piece was never uttered publicly, only written down. Calvin gives the reason for a second visitation: Egypt was punished not only for provoking God but for corrupting the Jews, and the word came while both were still secure. Henry states the justice of it plainly: those who encroached on others should be encroached on themselves.

The proclamation names cities. Gill takes it as notice of the invader's coming; Ellicott says the general summons is narrowed to his immediate objects. Clarke supplies the Greek equivalents of the three and reads the sword devouring round about of neighbouring peoples already flattened by Chaldean arms. Calvin rejects identifying the second with the great port, prefers the old capital, and denies it can be the first, since the prophet lists them separately. He also defends the manner: a plain statement would have been despised, so a forcible style was needed; unlike public speakers courting applause, the prophets meant to teach and threaten to some effect.

The question about the strong one is the hardest line in the tile. Gill takes the verb from a sweeping torrent and applies it to the force driving men from their posts. Keil and Delitzsch see the power already broken in spirit, note that the noun elsewhere describes stallions and bulls, and weigh whether men of war are meant, since the singular verbs that follow point to a singular noun the form resists. Ellicott cuts the knot: read it as thy strong bull dragged away, which the old versions support in number, the Greek making it the sacred bull that stood for the chief deity — so the line becomes the triumph of Israel's God over an animal god, fulfilled literally when a Persian conqueror killed the beast. Calvin lets the astonishment stand as rhetoric: unbelievers treat prophecy as fable and sleep over their prosperity, so they are asked how it happened, and answered that God drove them.

Then the foreigners run. Keil and Delitzsch leave the speakers indefinite and take them for strangers generally, not merely hired troops or allied nations. Clarke has ranks falling on ranks in terror, the fugitives being the auxiliaries. Ellicott thinks of settlers an earlier king had encouraged, or refugees from Judah, and records a Greek text that made the oppressing sword a Grecian one. Calvin supplies the unnamed subject, God, and observes that crowding alone would do the work, since before the enemy struck they would dash against one another; men who came for the land's richness would judge their own soil better.

The closing cry is disputed at every word. Gill assigns it to the auxiliaries in the field rather than to mocking Chaldeans or Egyptians complaining at home. Keil and Delitzsch fix the place as Egypt itself, argue that the noun means ruin rather than noise, and record the variant reading name for there, dismissing one rendering built on it as decidedly false. Ellicott surveys the same wreckage and prefers a slightly altered text: they have called the name of Pharaoh, A Noise, he has let the appointed season pass. Clarke prints a version in which the allies excuse themselves to their king because a tumult prevented the appointed meeting. Wesley keeps it simple: a great noise that came to nothing, and a day he fixed himself and let slip. Calvin hears soldiers who had believed the boasting, come to Pharaoh as to a god and finding a king of tumult.
18:
An oath opens the section, and Gill weighs the title behind it: a king greater than either of the two named, who swears by his own life because there is nothing greater. Calvin explains why an oath was needed. The delay had persuaded the Egyptians that the threat was false or forgotten, and the Jews had their own dismissals. God suspends punishment, he says, and the vengeance breaks out when the unbelieving least expect it.

The two mountains are agreed on and their application is not. Ellicott takes them for the invader in his high-towering greatness, one rising in solitary bulk above the plain and the other above the sea. Clarke, describing the first as standing alone and highest in its neighbourhood, turns the figure round: were the Egyptians as distinguished for valour as those hills for height, they could not stand the coming shock. Wesley takes it a third way, of encompassing: the enemy will surround them as surely as the one hill is ringed by mountains and the other by the sea.

The order to pack follows. Gill pictures inhabitants long settled in security; Clarke says only that the thing is unavoidable. Ellicott has the personified nation preparing with the instruments of captivity, and the old capital left depopulated. Calvin makes the tone deliberate provocation, since the unbelieving stay stupid unless their torpor is shaken out by force, and notes that the city sentenced to solitude was the one whose monuments were counted among the wonders of the world.

Then the heifer. Gill reads her as never yoked because never conquered, fat enough for slaughter; Keil and Delitzsch note the feminine chosen to match the personified nation and read the adjective as very beautiful rather than coquetting, the beast being a people well fed in a rich land. What comes from the north is disputed: the rare word points to pinching or nipping, yielding a stinging fly rather than plain destruction. Ellicott takes that reading and has the gadfly sting the heifer into the madness of agony, adds that the image points at the animal worship, the nation being like its god, and notes the Greek legend of a girl turned into a heifer and so tormented. Calvin says abundance is named because it blinds.

The mercenaries enter the figure as stalled bullocks. Gill has foreigners who lived so deliciously they were unfit for war, and reports the reading that makes them the princes in charge of the heifer. Keil and Delitzsch distinguish them from the allies named earlier and explain the comparison by the camps where the crown kept them well provided, since it depended on them. Ellicott makes them a drove of terrified cattle driven to the slaughter-house. Calvin observes that hired men look the more warlike, seeking war rather than meeting it from necessity, but soft living ruins soldiers.

The last figure is a hiss and an axe. Gill contrasts the bellowing of a heifer in fat pasture with the hiss of a serpent driven from its hole, and takes the voice for submission, not one big word to the conquerors; he cites the ancients for the thinness of that sound, and reports a reading that hears the serpents from far off. Calvin agrees the complaint would be no clamour but a mutter. Keil and Delitzsch call the clause difficult and reject the emendation that turns the verb into hissing. Ellicott has the serpent hissing in rage in the forest the enemy is entering, before the sign gives way to the thing signified and barbarous tribes appear with axes instead of swords, felling the trees that stand for Egypt's power; Wesley reads the axes the same way. The forest is Egypt's cities, which Clarke numbers at one thousand and twenty; Calvin renders the difficult clause as saying the forest cannot be searched out, which Wesley glosses as impenetrable.
24:
The figure is dropped and the thing said plainly. Gill has the kingdom, or its people, shamed before all nations and carried away; Clarke identifies the people of the north as the Chaldeans. Calvin adds the tone of the conquest, that the victors would be proud and treat the beaten reproachfully, and explains the repetition: the thing was incredible then, and the prophet was contending with settled unbelief.

The titles that introduce the sentence are given a reason. Gill reports the rabbinic explanation of God of Israel here, that the vengeance repaid the treatment of Israel by two of its kings. The god named next divides the voices over both halves of his name. Clarke reads it as the Egyptian name of their chief god, whose temple stood in the city the Greeks called after their own Zeus, the Thebes famous for a hundred gates. Ellicott prefers to punish Amon of No, taking the first word as the god's name with a play on its Hebrew sense of multitude, and puts the city in the south. Calvin takes the word in the Hebrew sense outright and puts the city elsewhere, at the port later renamed after its Macedonian founder — a part named for the whole.

The delivering up is short, and Calvin dwells on its words. To seek a life, he says, is exactly not to spare it, so the phrase declares how deadly the conquerors would be; and it degrades further that not the king only but his servants are named. Gill takes the sufferers to be the king, his people, and all who trusted him.

Then the sentence lifts. Clarke reports the promise of reinhabiting fulfilled within forty years, on a contemporary's authority. Ellicott hears the gleam of hope that ends other visions of judgment, and states the limit: Egypt was to revive, but never again stand among the conquerors of the world. Calvin is more careful. The restoration was not favour to a heathen nation but proof that God would not destroy it utterly; he notes that the other prophet makes the restored kingdom small and abject where this one seems to promise the old prosperity.

The last two verses turn to Israel, and Keil and Delitzsch mark them off as a promise. Calvin explains why one belongs at the end of an oracle about foreigners. The prophet was never appointed teacher of the nations, so all he said of them was said for his own people, who would otherwise have concluded that their case was worse than anyone's and the covenant a burden. Without the predictions, he adds, they would have watched judgment fall on their neighbours and called it chance. Henry states the purpose in a sentence: comfort and peace are spoken to the Israel of God while judgment is abroad among the nations.

The repetition at the close is deliberate. Gill takes it as consolation against the fear of being cast off, the presence promised to men still far off in captivity. Calvin says the repetition was needed because captivity was little short of death, and recalls their saying about whether God could raise the dead from their graves, answered in the vision of dry bones; the promise rests on gratuitous adoption alone, and the comparison in the last clause makes the sorrow bearable. Henry sets out its two halves, correction in measure on one side and no everlasting destruction on the other. Clarke reads it in the light of what followed: the city taken, the temple burnt, the people carried off, a seed still preserved. He quotes a writer who calls the survival of that people among the ruins of all their conquerors one of the most illustrious acts of providence: raindrops and rivers alike are lost in the sea, while this people flowed into every part of the world, mixed with all nations, and stayed separate from them all.
